text.brief: In 2004 Glenn Duffie Shriver, an American student in Shanghai, answered a newspaper ad that paid him $120 for an essay on relations between the United States and the People's Republic.
text.record: The woman who placed the ad introduced him to intelligence officers of the People's Republic, who paid him more than $70,000 over several years ([DOJ Office of Public Affairs release via FBI: Michigan man sentenced 48 months for attempting to spy for the PRC (January 21, 2011)](https://www.fbi.gov/washingtondc/press-releases/2011/wfo012111.htm)). At their direction he applied to the State Department's Foreign Service and then to the CIA's clandestine service. He pleaded guilty in October 2010 and received a sentence of 48 months in January 2011 ([DOJ release via FBI: Michigan man pleads guilty (October 22, 2010)](https://archives.fbi.gov/archives/washingtondc/press-releases/2010/wfo102210a.htm); [DOJ release via FBI: Michigan man sentenced to 48 months (January 21, 2011)](https://www.fbi.gov/washingtondc/press-releases/2011/wfo012111.htm)). The FBI later made his case into a training film called Game of Pawns.
text.reading: The officers started with a small payment for harmless work and raised the stakes by degrees, a gradient the recruit could justify one step at a time. The prize was the student's future access, which is Stratagem 17.
text.gapText: Application Architecture. The clearance routine held, and investigators stopped Shriver before he joined.
text.fix: Warn students before they go abroad about how approaches begin, and give them a safe path to report one without penalty.
